description: LunaLab is a two-person team developing an interactive lunar base engineering simulator. Our project aims to combine survival gameplay with educational missions, where players manage energy, life support, food production, and other essential systems while solving engineering challenges. Our goal is to make lunar engineering engaging and accessible.
summary: LunaLab is a browser-based educational game that lets young learners run a lunar outpost and explore the engineering trade-offs behind a space mission. Players build a solar array, oxygen generator, greenhouse, battery storage and storm shelter while managing energy, oxygen, food, supplies and crew safety. A five-chapter, 35-day story is followed by recurring missions. Science Academy lessons connect decisions to short readings and questions, with badges and in-game rewards. The oxygen budget uses a NASA planning estimate of 0.84 kg per person per day; an archived NASA DONKI solar particle event inspires a mission warning. Game timings and consequences are simplified and fictional. LunaLab aims to make space engineering understandable through decisions and their consequences.
details:
LunaLab is an educational lunar outpost simulator created for the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. It helps young learners explore the decisions involved in keeping a small crew safe on the Moon.

Players build facilities and manage energy, oxygen, food, supplies and crew safety. Each system creates trade-offs. For example, solar panels produce power in sunlight, while oxygen generation consumes energy. Before a long shadow, players must decide whether to charge the battery or use energy to produce extra oxygen.

The story has five chapters covering a solar particle warning, long shadows, dusty panels, a supply lander and an oxygen leak. After the 35-day story, the game continues with a rotating set of six mission types.

Science Academy contains nine short lessons with questions, hints and explanations. A correct answer earns a badge and in-game supplies. The lessons connect gameplay to topics such as power, life support, radiation protection and communication delays.

NASA’s crew-consumption estimate is used to calculate the daily oxygen needs of two astronauts. An archived NASA DONKI record of a solar energetic particle event appears in a lesson and inspires a fictional mission warning. The game does not provide a live space-weather forecast or calculate real radiation exposure. Its timings, equipment performance and safety points are simplified game values.

The prototype uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, runs in a web browser and saves progress locally. Automated checks cover core simulation behavior. Its educational impact has not yet been tested with children.

OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex generated and revised prototype code, educational text and original SVG artwork, and assisted with research. The participant selected the concept, guided the design and gameplay, and tested the prototype. AI-generated artwork is labeled in the game.
